utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Registrar, this is Monday, September 7, 2009, and I greet General Praljak, Mr. Pusic, Mr. Petkovic, Mr. Stojic, and Mr. Prlic. I also greet Defence counsels, Mr. Stringer, his colleague and everyone helping us. I would like to ask the Registrar to move into closed session because we will issue a decision, an oral decision but this needs to be done in closed session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In public session, let me say that we still have two binders to go through, binder number 10 and a new binder, binder number 11, which seems to be a binder with several documents. Mr. Stringer, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon. Good afternoon, Your Honours, counsel, everyone else in and around the courtroom. Mr. President, the eleventh binder is going to be the last binder, and with some luck we'll be able to move through that one today and complete the Prosecution cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, General.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, when we left off last week, I believe we were talking about Exhibit P04520, and can you find that document in your binder.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, on Thursday when we finished we were on the second page of the English version. I had asked you about the item that was the third bullet point on that page related to the Oerlikon, a weapon using 20-millimetre ammunition. Now -- so using that as a point of reference, I want to just sort of quickly go through the next few lines in this and then I'll ask you a few questions about it. And I'm going to be -- I'm going to start reading the next paragraph which begins with these words -- this is the -- about a quarter or a third of the way down from the top of page 2 of the English: "They were on the operational frequency of Mr. Mijo Jelic's military police, but all instructions were received from the South-East Herzegovina Operative Zone, PZO, which I believe is the anti-aircraft defence chief." Do you have that next, General? Are you able to follow along?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm looking for it. Just give me a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, if you're on page 2 of your version, the second -- the second point there refers to a PAT 20/1 Oerlikon. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And I'm moving down probably about six lines from that point: "They were on the operational frequency of Mr. Mijo Jelic's military police ..." do you have that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: "But all instructions were received from the South-East Herzegovina Operative Zone, chief of anti-aircraft defence." That's how I understand that to read. And then it goes on to talk about the crew who was firing on this position. I'm moving down. There's reference to people who had gone earlier by night to the northern part, observation post at Planinica, and then it continues: "We were all in contact by radio contact (Motorola). Cutuk had a direct connection to the military police." This is relating to the fire --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Cutuk. Not Citluk but Cutuk.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Cutuk. That's a person, right, not a place?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then going down it says: "According to a later report from Mr. Jelic's deputy, Mr. Dedo, they said that they had terrific support from the PZO weapons." And then it makes reference to a Muslim armed forces attack on the Bulevar health centre. And then just again skipping down and then towards the end of this paragraph it says: "We received constant instructions via the radio set from Bozic at the firing position where Mr. Lasic, Tuta, Bozic and others were about the appearance of vehicles and the need to open fire." Okay. So, General, all of that just to put this to you. What this shows in respect of the artillery that is deployed in this particular operation on the 25th of August, I believe, the day before this report was made shows a great deal of co-ordination and communication within the operative zone and the military police in respect of the artillery. Would you agree with me there?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what's described here is that they were in communication, but the 14.5 millimetre anti-aircraft guns, the PATs, P-A-T-S, were mostly infantry weapons. And secondly, the Motorolas that were used provided a very unsafe communication line easily tapped into so that the quality of that communication was not that good. Yes, the direct communication was, but the Motorolas were intercepted and scanners could detect the Motorolas frequency easily.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: But in any event what this tells us is that, at least in respect of this operation, there was good co-ordination and communication among the various HVO personnel who were involved. Would you agree with me there?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, to stay with this issue, General, I want to take you to -- actually, I'm going to skip the next document in your binder and I want to take you to P10960.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stringer, I have a follow-up question for General Praljak. It's a question which I could possibly also put to Mr. Coric's witness, but I might as well put it to you right away because it's a technical question. You might not be really able to answer, but we'll try. Using this document, we see that the military police has communication equipment at hand. Obviously they have Motorolas. And you said that the lines were not fully secure. The enemy was able to scan frequencies and eavesdrop. I'm sure that everyone agrees with you or can agree with you, but I have another question on another angle. The military police, if I understood you correctly, did not depend [as interpreted] from the Main Staff, was not subordinated to the Main Staff, and it has an internal communication system which must be regulated according to different radio frequencies that are allocated to different battalions of the said military police. However, when a unit of the military police is resubordinated to a brigade, I would like to know whether the military police in such a case keeps its own -- its frequencies, its radio frequencies or it changes its radio frequencies in order to be on the same radio frequency as the brigade that is now resubordinated to. Could you tell us exactly how this is organised, if you know, of course. Otherwise, just tell us that you don't know, that you cannot answer, and I'll wait for another witness to put my question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do know. It was very difficult for us to change frequencies, Your Honours, for the simple reason that the Motorolas had to be carried on -- well, you had to tap in the frequencies in a special way. So a certain number of Motorolas from the brigade military police or whatever were -- the frequencies went through channels. You had to key in the channels and then they would say go to channels in front, two up, two down, that kind of thing. So it was very difficult to change them, because any changes in frequency which were allotted to each channel was a very complicated matter for us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So the frequency was not changed. Even though they were resubordinated they would keep the same frequencies as before.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Probably they would have two Motorolas; one to function amongst ourselves and another one to be able to communicate with the other unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, your answer is technically acceptable. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, the next exhibit is P10960.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to make an objection with regard to the use of this document before we actually start using it. I'd like to explain why, with your permission, just three words on the subject. [In English] Praljak Defence, as a matter of principle, objects to the use of this document P10962, to prove the truth of the matter accepted therein. Hearsay, per se, is not forbidden at this Tribunal, but certain out-of-court statements are restricted by various rules and the statements and reports of experts are specifically restricted by Rule 94 bis. The Prosecution is on the record recently objecting to the admission of a book by Dr. Shrader which Praljak Defence used during the direct examination. They objected because they characterised this book as an expert report and that at that time the Prosecution asserted the Praljak Defence should have called him. This is exactly now my assertion when we are talking about this document. The Praljak Defence continues to submit that the book by Dr. Shrader, it is not an expert report, but there is no question that the document the Prosecution is now using or attempt to use is an expert report. By the Prosecution's own logic, this expert report cannot be introduced to prove the truth of the matter asserted therein without the full procedure outlined in Rule 94 bis. If the Prosecutor -- if the Prosecutor's use of the expert report is permitted in -- contrary to the rule of -- to the Rule 94 bis as a matter of equity, then Dr. Shrader's book clearly must come in. I mean, Dr. Shrader's book which we were using as so-called expert material. This is our -- this is our opposition, and we move to Chamber to first rule on the use of this material at all. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, good afternoon to you and everybody else in the courtroom. Objection from the Petkovic Defence at the attempt by the Prosecutor to use this material as being a fresh piece of evidence despite the cross-examination of General Praljak. Now, the Petkovic Defence objection is based on the decision made by the Trial Chamber on the 27th of November, 2008, by which it was established that the rule would be that the Prosecutor during the cross-examination of a Defence witness does not have the right to use new documents except to discredit the witness or to refresh his memory. With respect to the discreditation of the witness or to refresh the witness's memory, the original documents can be used, and this P10960 document that we're offered up here does not come under that category of documents; and therefore the Petkovic Defence objects to the use of that particular document and requests of the Trial Chamber to disallow the Prosecutor from answering -- from asking any questions with respect to that -- of that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, the -- it's possible that counsel for General Praljak misspoke the exhibit number, so just for the record, we're on P10960. And just by way of background, because I don't know that the Trial Chamber has seen this one before, the Trial Chamber will recall that the Praljak Defence called Dr. Slobodan Jankovic to testify as an expert witness in this case. He came and testified about the destruction or the collapse of the Old Bridge in Mostar on the 9th of November, 1993. Now, Dr. Jankovic prepared an additional report -- prepared two reports. One was about the Old Bridge, and the Trial Chamber has seen that report. He prepared a different report, which is the one that is in front of the Trial Chamber now, and that one was disclosed by the Praljak Defence to the Prosecution and all the parties, although it was not tendered into evidence by the Praljak Defence, and based on my -- it's my understanding that they do not intend to call Mr. Jankovic to testify about this particular report, this particular report being an analysis of the HVO artillery in the Mostar area. Now, what the Prosecution proposes to do, since this is an expert report prepared by someone at the request of the Praljak Defence, is to ask the general about a few parts of this and ask him to comment on those. I don't believe that the Prosecution's intention is to tender the entire report into evidence. We do think, however, that it's fair to put the Defence's own expert report to the general on cross-examination and use it to make some assertions and to cross-examine the general about HVO artillery as it's discussed in this report. So what I propose, Mr. President, is -- is, with your leave, to proceed with the cross-examination. There are just a few pages I'm going to ask the general about. We can take his answers and go from there, if you will. It may be the Prosecution tenders some pages, some excerpts of this into evidence, I don't know. We'll have to see how it goes. But in any event, the main purpose is to use it to cross-examine the general. It's a new document. The Prosecution never got it until it was disclosed to us by the Praljak Defence, so that's why it's not something that we would have had for -- certainly not on our 65 ter list that was filed before the trial began.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour. If I may just very, very briefly reply. I agree with the Prosecutor. It is material which we disclosed to the Prosecution. We disclosed it for fairness, bona fides, to inform in advance Prosecution about possible material we would later possibly filed under -- file under Rule 94 bis. We didn't. So it is not expert report, because only under Rule 94 bis if the procedure is respected then it could become expert report. So far it is not. And I would just simply like to ask Your Honour -- this Honourable Chamber to give us a ruling on the matter because of the reasons I said. This is not expert report, and it is only hearsay in that sense, and the Prosecution should not go into that document. And by the way, it wasn't used in any way, any such -- any similar document, let alone this one, during the direct testimony of Mr. Praljak. And Prosecution might have called this expert by their wish. This is why we gave them the material to inform them about the possibility. They didn't. They choose not to. Now they cannot circumvent this failure. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, may I just say something on behalf of the Petkovic Defence? May I respond, please? The explanation given to us by my learned friend Mr. Stringer for the use of this document boils down to the following: That the Prosecution wants to have either parts of this document admitted into evidence or to have part of the report through asking General Praljak questions and recording his answers that they become exhibits in this trial, admitted again. So the reasons given by Mr. Stringer do not relate to either the credibility of the witness or to refreshing the witness's memory, which were the reasons that were considered valid by the Trial Chamber for having a document admitted. Therefore, we consider that anything else goes against the grain of the ruling by the Trial Chamber in 2008 and that they are trying to, in fact, introduce a new document which holds the accused accountable in these proceedings. Now, the Petkovic Defence does not consider it to be a credible document, and, therefore, does not consider that the Trial Chamber should allow any questions to be posed on the basis of this document. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a second, please, Mr. Kovacic. I am slightly astonished for the following reason: You're saying the document P10960 is based on hearsay and that for you it means that it's a worthless document. However, as Mr. Stringer put it so well, you had requested initially that this report be admitted into evidence together with the other report which related on the destruction of the Old Bridge. So at -- initially, I thought I understood you saying that these were not rumours or hearsay, it was scientific. So the report that we have now was not admitted or had not been admitted into file when the Old Bridge issue arose. However, now we have this document, and the Prosecutor wanted to use this document which stems from you. I don't know which questions he wishes to put to the witness through this document, but he wished to use the document. I briefly looked at the document, and I was under the impression that the purpose of this document, based on mathematical formulas, talks about various trajectories of shells or bullets according to various trajectories, and basically this report relates to that. So when you are asking that Professor Jankovic be recognised as a witness, you put that in your file, and today when the Prosecutor wishes to use this document, you state that Jankovic's work, and he's certainly going to be pleased about it, is based on hearsay. So I really don't understand a thing any more. I don't understand what you are saying. Maybe there was an interpretation mistake somewhere, but I absolutely do not understand what you are telling us, because a few months ago you were telling us that this was an excellent report and now you're telling us that it's completely worthless. So please tell us what you wanted to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it's probably my mistake. Perhaps I was not clear or something maybe was lost in translation, I don't know, but it is my assertion that this document, in procedural terms, now, at this point, can be considered as hearsay evidence. Why? Because it is not an expert report. [In English] This not the expert report. It could have become exert report only if procedure prescribed under Rule 94 bis is fully respected, and it was not. We have never filed this material, Professor Jankovic material, as an expert report. We did request expert to make some analysis for us internally, for the Defence, and we also went a step further. We were -- we are, by ethics, required, or at least this is what we think, to give this material to the Prosecution at this -- at that time, because we thought that there is a possibility that we would respect Rule 94 bis and that we would file this report as expert report. However, we choose not to, and because it is not filed, it is material which now could only be hearsay, because the Prosecution said this is the expert report. It is not expert report. It cannot be expert report. We are missing the procedure under Rule 94 bis. However, however, Your Honours, however, if the Prosecution want to have this as expert report, Dr. Jankovic is available. His address is in the file. He was here. The Prosecutor could always move and try to observe procedural rules and try to -- to submit this material as expert report. Unless it is not done, it is hearsay, the same as articles or some other. But my major point is that I was trying -- or we, this Defence, was trying to do the same thing with the Shrader book on the beginning of General Praljak testimony, and we were not allowed. Dr. Shrader is not an expert. This is what the Prosecution said. It is in the record. Dr. Shrader is not an expert. So now I said Dr. Jankovic is not an expert. In procedural sense, no, he is not, and we cannot use that material under this adjective. Thank you so much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honours, before Mr. Stringer were to answer all of us, perhaps it might be convenient if I were just to comment on an observation that Your Honour made a few minutes ago. It's our submission that it's absolutely irrelevant whether there had been an application to introduce this report into evidence. The fact is it is not in evidence, and either it is or it isn't, and the application of Your Honours' decision of the 27th of November, 2008, and all the other principles is not affected by the question of whether there had been an application. That's enough on its own to deal with the point, but I would just add that after all, it was only an application by one of the accused. It wasn't an application by any of the rest of us and it's not likely that the Prosecution is going to seek to use this material only against one accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stringer, before I give you the floor, the Chamber would like to know the following. This is actually a request made by my colleague, but everybody agrees in this Trial Chamber. For which purpose do you wish to use this document exactly?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: To question the general on the HVO's use and capabilities in its deployment and use of artillery in the Mostar area as indicated in this report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So if I understand correctly, you wish to use this document to find out how the HVO used the artillery in the Mostar area?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And the extent to which they -- the weaponry -- they were qualified and trained and were able to use the weaponry correctly. Mr. President, if I could just quickly respond.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I'm looking at the Slobodan Praljak's, and this is a quote, Slobodan Praljak's submission of the expert reports of Slobodan Jankovic, filed publicly in this case on the 9th of May, 2008. All right? It's a public filing, and we know that those two reports are the report on the Stari Most, the Old Bridge, and this one. That's number one. And maybe I didn't speak clearly enough. It's a new document. That is to say, we never saw this until the 9th of May, 2008, so this document came into possession of the Prosecution after the Prosecution had closed its case. So it's new. It's not something that we had before. So the limitations that are being pushed by the Petkovic team don't apply, in our -- in our view, Mr. President. But in any event, whether it's an expert report, whether it's a book, whether it's a paper, we've all sat through many hours in this courtroom of -- and we sat through many hours of the Praljak Defence bringing any number of books and writings to the fore, questioning the general about them. The general was holding forth on a lot of books, the books written by Mr. Filipovic, Mr. Agic, others, and I think for anybody to suggest that the Prosecution is not able to use this particular document which we received from the Praljak Defence itself, and to use it as a basis for putting questions to the general, I think it has no foundations -- completely unfair based upon the practice that we've had throughout this trial, and on top of that, it is a new document. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me confer with my fellow Judges.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if you allow me two sentences regarding the term "new document." From your decision it is quite clear, and also from the Rules of Procedure and Evidence of this Tribunal, it is quite clear what can and what cannot be considered a new document. A new document is never an item that the Prosecution had in its position during its case. To use such a document during the Defence case would be considered acting in contravention of due diligence. A new document is always a document that the Prosecution obtained after it has rested its case or a document that for justifiable reasons could not have been used the course of its case, and it is spelled out quite clearly in the November 2008 decision of the Trial Chamber. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let me confer with my fellow Judges.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The Chamber will render its oral decision about this. The Trial Chamber would like to remind the parties that it rendered a decision on the 27th of November, 2008, in which it states in paragraph 20 and 21 of the same decision that, I quote: "Only for exceptional reasons -- only exceptional reasons allow to derogate from the interest of justice according to Article 94 bis of the Rules, such as an importance of a new document." Therefore, if the Prosecution wishes to file after the presentation of its case new documentation in order to establish the guilty -- guilt of one or more accused, it must explain to the Chamber how and -- how they obtained the documents. The Trial Chamber notices that these documents were communicated to the Prosecution after the request pertaining to the report of Professor Jankovic. The Trial Chamber, therefore, notes that the Prosecution was in possession of this document after it -- after they presented their case. Therefore -- or furthermore, the Trial Chamber would like to remind the parties of paragraph 21 of its decision when -- where the Trial Chamber stated that if the Trial Chamber decided to establish new documents in order to prove the guilt of the accused in the interest of justice, they must allow Defence to -- the Defence to challenge its proof and its evidence. This is why we can give the Trial Chamber [as interpreted] more time in order to present irrefutable evidence, and the Trial Chamber could also allow an additional cross-examination. The Trial Chamber notes that today we are at the stage of the cross-examination led by the Prosecution, and following this cross-examination, additional questions will arise, and these additional questions will enable the Defence to put all useful questions on the span of this document. Furthermore, at this stage of the procedure, the Trial Chamber believes that the Trial Chamber is not right now facing the admission of the document by the authorisation, given by the Prosecutor, to put questions by using the document. Therefore, the Trial Chamber authorises the Prosecutor to put questions through this document or on the basis of this document, and if later on the Prosecutor requests the filing of this document into evidence, the Trial Chamber will, of course, examine at that time the observations presented by the Defence on the question of the admissibility of the document. And to conclude, the Trial Chamber authorises Mr. Stringer to put questions to Mr. Praljak based on the document. Thank you. Mr. Stringer, go ahead. It's your floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, while we've been talking, have you had a few minutes to look at the document?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Stringer, that's not enough time for me to look at a document of this size. It should have been given to me in advance, but all right, I will.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Let me ask you a more specific question. Do you recognise this document? Did you see it before, before today?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I just leafed through it. I browsed through it. A long time -- well, I wasn't really familiar with this document. I wasn't really studying this document in depth. I think I had -- well, it was said that the document would not be tendered into evidence, and I really didn't look at it that closely.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Did you provide Dr. Jankovic with -- with documents and things that he used to make this report?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I just want to ask you about a few parts of this document. We're not going to go through it in great detail. In his first section at the very beginning, section one on the level of training of artillery crews, I want to turn to -- General, in your version, the original language version, it's the bottom of page 1, and this is the bottom of page 2 of the English, and it says: "In the HVO artillery units, there were few men who had been recruits in the former country's army and undergone artillery training for any kind of weapon in the ROs," which I believe here is indicated to be reserve officer schools, "and even fewer who had been trained for the weapon they were operating in the HVO." General, would you agree with that statement based upon your knowledge during the time you were commander of the HVO Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't do any such analysis. I didn't do any such analysis, so -- and I cannot testify to that effect. And we can see here that Mr. Jankovic -- well, I read an excerpt and the fact and because he teaches at military academy, he teaches artillery, and he knew that the Croats -- well, that they responded in small numbers, and even if they did, Croats were not usually deployed in artillery. Well, that's his experience, but I think that the personnel in the artillery were mostly -- mostly, well, they had the appropriate speciality and training. At least the chief of artillery had appropriate training. I don't know whether all of them had gone --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Let's --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- through this training in JNA, but at any rate, they were trained in the HVO, because we did run courses, as you could see from the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, it says -- continues on: "An HVO artilleryman who had undergone training as a recruit in the former army would have done so some 10 years previously, and thus would have forgotten most things." And then he continues: "There were very few professional officers in the HVO (engineers or graduate weapons engineers). To my knowledge, there was only one officer in the HVO who was a graduate weapons engineer." And it goes on, and I'm going to skip the next sentence and then he says: "Even the HVO command [Realtime transcript read in error "chain of command"] lacked sufficient specialist military knowledge, because in most cases, for security reasons, HVO officers were men who had no connection with the former Yugoslav Army." General, would you agree with the assessment here of Dr. Jankovic that the HVO command lacked sufficient specialist military knowledge in respect of its artillery?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can give you the same answer again. The chief of the HVO, General Petkovic, served in the JNA in the artillery. He was a gunner. So I cannot really give you an answer to this question, but I wouldn't agree with what I see here. Well, right at the beginning, Mr. Stringer, at the beginning of the war with the Serbs where I served in Sunja and so on, it is true that there were some things that could have been considered as lack of appropriate training for mortars, which was the only thing that we had at the beginning. We didn't have anything else. But I think that the artillery did its job properly. It knew how to do its job, in particular in light of the fact that using 203-millimetre cannon -- well, they were never used to fire anywhere near Mostar, because if it had hit any of the buildings, it would have just torn them down, pulverised them. So it was really very --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, General, we established, I think, at the beginning of your cross-examination that you were only a member, yourself, of the JNA for about three months before you were released on this medical grounds that we discussed: So the fact is you never had any training yourself in artillery, did you, before you took command of the HVO Main Staff, formal training that is?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's correct. I didn't have any training in the artillery, but as an engineer who knows all about azimuths and elevations and initial speed and range and so on, you could not say that I was an expert, but I knew the difference between different kind of cannon, howitzers and so on, the basic elements of their use. I knew that regardless of the fact it had nothing to do with the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Excuse me. Could I -- just before it disappears on the page. It's at page 20, line 19, the words "chain of" seem to have slipped in. The report in our translation doesn't say the HVO chain of command. I'm not suggesting it affects the price of fish terribly much in the long-run but those words aren't in the original report. It just says HVO command.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: That's correct. I don't know if I misspoke or whether it just leaked into the transcript. It says "even the HVO command lacked sufficient specialist military knowledge."

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, just to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a second, please. General Praljak, for those who in their military life had to participate at a fire exercise with, let's say, a 155-millimetre cannon, 203-millimetres, know that it's very complicated; right? The Prosecutor states that you had a three-month training in the JNA, but, General Praljak, if you were placed behind a 203-millimetre cannon, would you be able to make it work, and would you be able to send a shell on a particular target? Would you be able to do that yourself even if you know the mathematical formulas?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you very much. That's what I thought.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, just to continue. This is about the middle of the page number 2 now of your version, and this is about the middle of page 3, a little bit below. It says: "All of this -- all this clearly indicates that the HVO artillery was founded on knowledge that the men had to acquire through short courses lasting just a few days, or even just pick up themselves on the spot, from one day to the next. Therefore, they were not in a position to apply firing rules, and were not fully able to use firing tables or the procedures required to hit a particular target, while specialist concepts such as fork, screening height, crest of defilade, parallax of target ..." and I'll skip the rest, "... remain unknown not just to the crews but also to many who were directing artillery fire. The consequences of these facts were serious." Now, General, you made reference to these courses in training in the HVO. Is that what Dr. Jankovic is referring to here when he talks about the short courses that they had to get some artillery training?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Stringer, a great part of this could refer to 1992 as regards Bosnia and Herzegovina, but I don't think that it could refer to 1993. Yes, there were courses that were needed to training people to operate this, but, of course, you had to take into account that we did not have a state that created an army. We had the people that became an army and then the state was formed. If an international community or NATO managed to put a stop to this war, then some things would have -- could perhaps have been done, but we were attacked and we defended ourselves as best we could in the face of the attack lest we should all be slaughtered. So yes in 1992, but not for 1993. I think by that time the HVO artillery was already, well, not up to the standards put forward by Professor Jankovic, but I'm sure that it was good enough to operate. Of course give or take the deviations that are allowed in artillery for mortars. For instance, if you have a firing table with the point targets, there is a great deal of dispersion there. So I was aware of that. I looked at that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right. So --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a correction perhaps at page 23, line 12, the answer is here recorded as being given by His Honour, Judge Antonetti. I think it should be corrected.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, General, the fact is -- I'm -- counsel's -- counsel is right, obviously. I think the transcript will be corrected on that. General, the fact is that the army that you commanded was one in which its artillery people were not sufficiently trained and the urgency of the situation required them to take use of artillery even though they weren't able to apply all the necessary firing techniques; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They did apply everything necessary, all the necessary techniques, but the guns which the JNA had, and I read that even those didn't have good firing tables translated from the NATO weapons that arrived in Yugoslavia in the 1950s when there was that clash with Russia. Eight or 9.000 cannons were provided then by the USA to Yugoslavia should it need to defend itself against the Soviet Union. But those tables were translated into Russian and then from Russian and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: So there were errors necessarily. And so it is true there was no high professionalism. However, all the necessary techniques --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, Mr. Praljak.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, well, I have to answer --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General -- Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: You've asked me so --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: -- the General has gone way beyond the scope of my question. It's just wasting my time here, the time I've got remaining. So, General, I'm going to ask you to focus so that we can get through this today.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, you've raised the issue of the HVO's weaponry, so let's talk about that a bit, and I'm going to go now to the top of page 3 of your version, General, and the bottom quarter of page 4 of the English, and this is in section 2. In a third paragraph Dr. Jankovic writes: "The HVO artillery was not systematically organised at all, and it is well known that the artillery comprises a system of weapon, projectile, fire control system, and logistics. The system of fire control is particularly sophisticated, and the effectiveness of artillery fire largely depends on it." Now, General, we've -- this report's about Mostar, but we've talked about HVO artillery in a number of locations such as on the Makljen Ridge. The fact is, General, isn't it true that the HVO did not possess the sophistication, the training necessary to use its artillery in a way that would distinguish sufficiently between civilian and military targets?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Incorrect. I don't know why you've mentioned Makljen and Mostar since that's at a distance of some 40 kilometres. And secondary -- secondly, the artillery was different and precisely because it was not sophisticated, yes, that is true, it wasn't highly sophisticated and precisely for that reason because it wasn't on a par with the NATO forces requirements, it was strictly prohibited to use the artillery to shoot where civilian targets were close by, and Mostar wasn't within a mortar's range, and -- within the range of certain guns, but just to the left and the right where the BH Army was expected to attack in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, continuing on, this is still on page 3 of the Croatian version, top of page 4 -- or excuse me, page 5 of the English, Dr. Jankovic continues on and then he concludes: "The lack of expertise as such that the attitude was 'if you have a weapon and ammunition, you have everything you need to carry out task.'" Now, is that how it was, General, during the time you were commander of the HVO? You had personnel in the HVO who possessed weapons, ammunition and everything except the technical expertise to use the weapon properly?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that wasn't how it was at that time, and it would be a good thing if Professor Jankovic would state the period of time that he was referred to, because he worked on training, as far as I know, the training of artillery men. He participated in that. Now, of course, at the beginning, and he says -- he's talking about the Croatian Army. Well, the people were under attack, and if they managed to come by -- people managed to come by something, they would shoot. But anyway, a system was put in place to train personnel, and you've seen many documents to that effect, to train people to utilise the weapons, and as time went by things improved. And Professor Jankovic worked in this area of training and you should have asked him.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well he's your -- or he made this for you, General, or your team. I'm assuming it relates to relevant time frames and locations to this case since it was made at the request of your team. Now, one last couple of questions on this.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, just continuing from where we left off, he identifies artillery pieces used by the HVO, and we see them all there. Then he identifies some additional weapons that had been from the former JNA, some of which had come from World War II. Two-hundred -- 203-millimetre M2 or M2A1, the H55, T 88, T 76. He says: Their barrels had already fired the maximum number of projectiles. After this number of projectiles, the barrels have greatly reduced muzzle velocities by over 5 per cent and thereby reduced range, but the main reason these barrels are unusable is the greatly increased dispersion of trajectories, making it difficult to hit a target with any kind of technical firing. Other words were given here in this translation. In artillery practice this is called the ballistic death of the barrel. Now, General, the fact, is at least in respect of these HVO guns, the HVO was not able to use these guns in a way that could distinguish sufficiently between civilian and military targets, isn't that true, because they were old guns that should not have been used at all?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could my learned friend rephrase the question, because he did precisely what we objected to to begin with, "The fact is that," et cetera, et cetera, or is that fact established. [In English] This is not an expert report, so it should be changed. The question must be changed. It is not established fact. It is simply opinion of professor in the material which did not became any official document. It was draft submitted to us, to the Defence, to see what -- what do next, and we decided not to use the document. So it is not the fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I can rephrase, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Looking at these -- the weapons that are identify here, General, would you agree generally that Jankovic identifies correctly what the HVO's artillery was during 1993?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he identified them correctly because they were artillery pieced used by the Yugoslav People's Army and then it was used subsequently by all sides except some guns which had the D30, 122-millimetre howitzers. Those were from Vitez and they were good ones and I think the 152 or whatever, 155.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And would you agree that among those pieces that the HVO used, some of them had actually come from the World War II era?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And would you also agree that the HVO was using old guns such as those from World War II even though they were no longer usable -- let me rephrase the question. Dr. Jankovic refers here to the ballistic death of the barrel. General, it is true that the HVO was using artillery pieces even including those which had encountered or undergone this ballistic death because they had been used so much before?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. Every barrel or every gun has a booklet attached to it stating how much it's been used, how many firings had been made and what the deviation can be when the piece is new and when it's used. And I don't know any of those facts except to say that I do know that it was a weapon used by all three sides in the war on the territory of the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Will you agree with me that those booklets you refer to, the HVO did not have those booklets for a number of its artillery pieces? Nobody actually knew how many times the barrels had been fired.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't agree with that. I think that there were books in existence, and I think that there were tables too. And Mr. Jankovic says here that for the 203, the tables were revised from the NATO standard to other standards. But anyway, if you didn't have the tables, you certainly didn't do any firing.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, I've got one -- there may be one discrepancy in this -- in this translation, and with the President's permission, I'd like to ask you to read part of this sentence so we can get it correctly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: May I refer to a misprint in the transcript on page 28, line 25. We read that about ballistic death, which is understandable, but I think it was ballistic gap or something that you had spoken about.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: No, it's death.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: It was death.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: It's the word that comes from the Jankovic report here, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Oh, excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: In fact, maybe --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, just so that we've got it correctly, staying with this paragraph we were just looking at, there's a sentence that begins with, "After this number of projectiles ..." do you see that? "After this number of projectiles ..." It says: "After this number of projectiles, the barrels have greatly reduced muzzle --"

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. "After this number of projectiles, the barrels have greatly reduced muzzle velocities by over 5 per cent and thereby reduced range." Do you want me to read on?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: "But the main reason these barrels are unusable is the greatly increased dispersion of trajectories, making it difficult to hit a target with any kind of -- using any kind of firing technique."

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right. And why don't you read the last sentence, just ...

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: "In artillery practice, this is called ballistic death of the barrel."

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, General, is that how it was with the HVO's -- at least the weapons indicated in this report that the HVO was not able to use a known or acceptable targeting technique that could distinguish sufficiently between civilian and military targets because these weapons were so old and overused?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Stringer. All this is in general terms here, but certain barrels, among other things, were renewed in Novi Travnik, and that's the process that we call calibration. They were recalibrated. And I know about this because I discussed the issue with the director of the factory, and the mortars were good anyway, and the 155-millimetre howitzers were in order, and the 122-millimetres, and all the mortars and the cannon. This could, perhaps, have applied to a 203-millimetre cannon. However, I'm not even sure about that one, whether the Yugoslav People's Army fired from that particular weapon after having received a large number from the Americans and then had this ballistic death of the barrel which is mentioned here.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I've finished with this document unless the Trial Chamber has questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, this is an interesting document, because it raises a number of questions. It's also interesting, because obviously the author of this document seems to be well-versed in artillery. You noted his conclusion in the last paragraph of the document on the use of artillery in Mostar. According to him, he concludes that computers were -- would have been necessary for the firing on - the HVO had no computers - that there was also a need for a logistical support which it didn't have, and that the weather system should also have been used, and you did not have this weather system available. According to him these are three prerequisites, and these prerequisites were not met. Given this, the Prosecutor insisted on the problem of civilian and military targets, and I already put questions to you on this. When one finds out that artillery pieces are located, for example, 8 kilometres or 5 kilometres from Mostar with a range that is under that, and so in order to increase the range, you have to increase the firing angle because of the parabolic trajectory, then you end up with something that is not very accurate, and how can you make sure that you can have an accurate fire, and how can you adjust your fire, you know, so it's accurate when you know, you know, you're shooting on a city where you will have civilians that are very close to the military, sometimes just a few metres away. This is what this artillery specialist is saying in his report. So how -- what's the solution to this problem? Given that the artillery that the HVO had was it possible for them to be accurate in their fire in order to make sure that there was no collateral damage inflicted on civilians when everybody knew that the military and the civilians were intermingled? Remember, General Praljak, earlier, you can take a look at the transcript, earlier it asked you whether before the fire there wasn't somebody with binoculars checking the target to see, you know, where the military fire was and where the civilians were before giving the go-ahead and allowing the fire to go. I asked this question earlier, and I haven't given a very close look at this document before, but now I have. If I had had this document before I put this question to you, I would have add this parameter. How did you manage when you had civilians close to the military just a few metres away? How could you make sure that your fire was so accurate that you would spare the civilians and really only shoot at the military. And another situation, which is almost what the specialist seems to say, was it that you just had a weapon, ammunition, and that was all you needed to carry out the task? Were you aware of that problem at least?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, that's not you how it was, Judge Antonetti, Your Honour, and we were all conscious of certain problems. There was not a single gun, cannon, however new in the world, or any crew able to hit a target in the way you have described it, 10 metres, 20 metres. I have already provided you with the NATO tables, and they show what a hit means. If you have a 120-millimetre mortar with projectiles and barrels that are in order, that they hit 50 metres away from a target, that is considered to be a perfectly good hit. Why? Because it's an anti-infantry weapon. And to use a cannon to fire at a distance of 20 kilometres, well, you would have to look at the meteorological conditions. Well, that's a very technical matter. There's no army that can know where the wind is blowing from, where it's raining and so on. That's just professional and theoretical and not something that you would find in -- when you have a war on your hands. But, Your Honours, that's why we didn't target Mostar. These are just stories going round that we targeted Mostar. Had we done so, there would have been thousands of dead. And I keep repeating the same thing over and over again. We even kept cannons at a distance from Mostar, and these multiple-barrel launchers, for example, they, by nature of the weapon they are, they have a 200 and 300 dispersion range, because it is not their aim to hit a target directly but to have a dispersion. Had we used these launchers to target Mostar, that would have meant and entailed hundreds of dead. So first of all, the cannons and guns were not that bad, nor were we that badly trained. And secondly, we didn't target anywhere in Mostar, but very precisely a target that had to be at a relative distance, as far away from civilians as possible. And had we targeted their mortars which were placed around the hospital or their Main Staff and all the rest of it with the 203-millimetre cannons, there would have been general devastation. Multiple-rocket launchers, A, they were in proper working order. Oganj, Plamen, and the third one, they were all good, and the Rak. The 130, the 152, the 122-millimetres, they were all good. They had new barrels or had not been used a lot. The 203-millimetre, well, that's another matter, but we took a great deal of care there too. And if we add up all the projectiles fired from all these weapons, there weren't that many.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, on line 11, page 33, you mentioned the 120-millimetre mortar, and you recognise that the use of this 120-millimetre mortar is such that there can be a 50-metre error in the targeting, but it's still considered as a perfectly good hit. Now, what exactly is 50 metres? It's the distance between Mr. Prlic at the back of this room and our court reporter. So somebody using 120-millimetre mortar, which has -- with an uncertainty of 50 metres means that if we target the military target, which is our court reporter, the civilian which is in the other side of the room could be hit. That's what you're saying, and you're saying it's a good hit. It's normal it. It's acceptable.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's what it says, what is written in your army, too, Judge Antonetti, and NATO. That's a hit. You can't do better than that. That's what NATO considers a hit. Had I provided you with the tables -- or, I provided with you with the tables and their evidence of what a hit is. It's not something where you have missed your target. It's a hit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let's assume that what you're saying is right. I don't see why I would challenge it. You say that this corresponds to NATO tables, which means that any army, whether it's Russian Army, the American Army, NATO, HVO, any of these armies using 120 metres -- 120-millimetre mortar could use this weapon even if there is a civilian that is standing by 50 metres from the military target. They're allowed to shoot.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct. With a cannon which is in good working order. For example, 130-millimetres at a distance of 20 kilometres. You have to fire 5.000 projectiles in order to hit a tank, a point target. And nobody can improve on that. It's the law of probability, because it's a thousand of a thousandth of a millimetre. So 5.000 projectiles you have to use according to the law of probability to be certain that you're going to hit a point target at a distance of 20 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So according to you, there's always a risk of inflicting collateral damage on civilians whenever there's a military -- whenever there's military fire.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely. Well, I don't dare compare, but if you compare the aerial bombings -- well, with lasers, laser guided. Errors are absolute. There's no army in the world which well, errors -- errors are incorporated into the probability, the probability of dispersion regardless of what kind of barrel you have. It's enough to have 10 grams more of gunpowder or that humidity is greater and you wouldn't have dispersion. It's unavoidable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me finish this off because what you're saying is quite complex, brings a lot to mind. So the well-trained firing artillery officer, well-trained, for example, trained in the JNA, because it seems that according to this specialist that we have here the JNA had excellent -- excellent training for the -- for their officials. He knows that there are civilian and military. He knows that the civilians are about a hundred metres from the military target. He just knows it because it's an urban target. So he knows that there will be civilians. But even though he knows that there is presence of civilians, is he allowed to shoot? If, of course, he is given the order to shoot. Is he supposed to execute the order?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He opens fire if he's a military target, and it depends on many factors. Judge Antonetti, Your Honour, after the first shell that falls somewhere, the alarm is sounded and all the civilians have to take refuge because the alarm is sounded, and the alarm is given that artillery fire is going to ensue. It says this on every building within the frameworks of civilian protection. The civilians have to take refuge. So depending on whether somebody's attacking you and by destroying their Main Staff you, of course, carry on firing and give the order to destroy the military target. The civilians have to be moved aside and the fighting continues among soldiers, among armies, between armies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're bringing in a new element, if I understood you correctly, but I don't have the firing instructions with me, you know, but normally before there should be a warning shot, before you actually shoot, you shoot a warning shot to tell civilians to go and take shelter, and it's only after that first shot that there is -- that the military target is truly targeted. According to you there is always a first warning shot. Is that it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A warning shot, as far as I know, must be fired and after that, civilians must seek shelter and then the firing may continue. I just wanted to let you know, Your Honours, that we used the 130-millimetre cannon which was positioned up on the Hum hill. We could, without the elevation points or anything, fire directly as you do with a rifle, target every single house in Mostar had we wanted to do that. No azimuths, no firing tables, no elevations or anything. We could fire at them from a rifle. It's a small distance, 2, 3 kilometres. We could have destroyed any target there. Had the HVO wanted to destroy Mostar, it would have been a different story.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I think it's time for the break, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was caught up in this topic, and I didn't look -- watch the clock, but we'll break for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stringer, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, I want to move on to the next document in the binders, 3D00793. And I think you'll recognise this. This is one of your exhibits. It's dated the 7th of November, 1993, Tomislavgrad, and it's a -- it appears to be the conclusions reached by various HVO commanders at the operative zone level or below, and I'm suggesting that to you based on the names that appear at the end of it. And it's -- the conclusions are then directed to the various entities indicated: President of Croatian Republic Herceg-Bosna, parliament, the government of Croatian Republic Herceg-Bosna, and then the Main Staff of the armed forces. And, General, this relates to a meeting that took place on the 7th of November among the various commanders, and they lay out these conclusions. General, the question to you is, are you -- were you present at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And could you tell us what was the purpose of the meeting?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The purpose of the meeting is described in the conclusions -- or, rather, in -- well, what -- what one could term -- well, the problems that are enumerated here, the problems that the military wing of the HVO was facing. So all those elements that prevented or affected the -- well, what we could call the improvements of the efficiency and the structure of the army. Well, it's all spelt out quite clearly here.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Would you agree with me, General, that this meeting took place at a period of time shortly after or at the time that Vares fell to the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, that would be the time period.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And were these conclusions, then, to the best of your knowledge, were they indeed forwarded on to the various bodies that are indicated in the head of the document?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, yes, they were forwarded.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, at this meeting, General, do you recall whether there was any discussion of any specific military operations or objectives that needed to be achieved?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the objectives were well-known at this meeting, and that was to defend ourselves. Our goal was to wage a defensive war against the army attacking us. Unfortunately, at this time it was the BH Army. Well, I don't know exactly what was discussed at the meeting, but the essence of it was that we listed elements and that the commanders of operational zones and of the brigades listed all the problems that they were bothered by, problems that affected or prevented them from exercising command or carrying out their tasks, and their tasks was to defend. So the command and control of the army, effective command and control of the army and everything else that is necessary for an army that is properly structured and that such an army must have.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Was Brigadier Petkovic also present at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Do you know where he was at the time?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection I think that Mr. Petkovic -- well, I don't know whether it was on that day or the next day. I think it was on that day he asked me after the return from Central Bosnia, to let him have a leave of absence of a couple of days because he was exhausted. He wanted to visit his family in Split, and I approved his leave, less than he requested, but I did approve his departure.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Do you recall whether at this meeting there was any discussion of switching from defensive actions to taking a more offensive posture and -- and, in fact, launching offensive actions against the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Had I been able to do that, I would have done that, Mr. Stringer, for a very simple reason, because the theatre of war is an integral thing, and if you are being attacked in Central Bosnia, in Vares and so on, then it is necessary to undertake offensive action, smaller or larger scale, in order to link up your forces so that they cannot mass their forces and take your territory piecemeal after signing a peace agreement, a cease-fire agreement with the Serbs so that they could deploy their units where they wanted to.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, just to stay with this, then, if we could move to the next exhibit, P0 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: May I ask a question. Mr. Praljak, you say you were present there. Why is your name not mentioned in the -- in the list of persons who are behind this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, since the commanders had already presented a number of problems, objections, complaints and so on, the meeting was convened by me, I attended it, and I did not consider -- well, because it was their initiative, and then I said, Okay, let's convene this meeting. We'll make a list of problems, and then you can send this to the Main Staff where I was. And that's why I didn't sign it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. And the second question: Number 6 demands the establishment of one and only command line. Could you explain what this refers to? What was the weakness that was to be amended by that point?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Judge Trechsel, it was simply the fact that many people in the municipalities -- well, we've discussed this at length here, they were able to finance the brigade in their municipality, and they influenced the appointment of commanders, and they interfered with the chain of command, and it made it impossible to have a single chain of command. To put it quite simply, somebody could simply leave the front line, go back to their municipality, and then efforts were made in any which way we could to -- or rather they did everything they could to prevent the punishment of that person. The municipal authorities would stand behind that person. They were on the payroll down there, and the chain of command was seriously affected and obstructed in this manner. In other words, your orders were not complied with, and it was impossible to punish anyone for it. The sanctions could not be enforced, which means that the chain of command was disrupted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Praljak. I had envisaged this possibility. I wondered whether there were other problems within the army regarding line of command, but I take your answer as meaning that it was the only problem that this refers to.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, as regards item 1 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me. I am exclusively referring to point 6 here, and there you say one and only command line because there were problems with municipalities. I remember, you are quite right, we have spoken about this a lot. The question is, were there any other problems with the command line or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, here all those items affected the chain of command. Item 2, as well, which is linked with the other one. Please appoint a single commissioner in the municipality who would then be in charge of it. There were too many interests there. Thievery, smuggling, municipal authorities, and it all disrupted the general principle in which an army is based.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, line 6, in fact, you've already told us that the municipal authority was sometimes having control over the military units, and this is why, of course we have this point 6, but after I heard your answer, I was wondering was there not maybe another problem, and that would be the command chain existing between Boban and the units. You've said it yourself, actually, Naletilic-Boban. According to you, was Naletilic within the chain of command? So if we take this hypothesis, I was just wondering if this document is not a putsch organised by a few officers against Boban to make him understand that things could not continue this way any more and that this document is there to remind him the principle of the command, which goes from the top to the bottom without having a double chain of command or line of command. So I'm just wondering if we read this line 6.6, was this not there maybe to go back to something that was perhaps not done in a correct way because it goes back to your own chain of command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct, Your Honour Judge Antonetti. To be quite frank, it is true. Well, regardless of what was understood under those units Tuta was not under the Main Staff, and for the most part this is what it refers to. It is true, Your Honours, that this smells of a coup. Of course -- well, my thought was either things would be changed along those lines or we would continue losing, and we would have all the problems that are concomitant with it, smuggling of coffee, cigarettes, alcohol, drugs, drug use. People would spend 20 days on the front line in the trenches, and then you can see somebody who got rich and was not sanctioned for it, and he says to this guy, "Well, you fool, are up there fighting." So the whole organisation had to be strengthened, organisation, in the municipalities, and to tell you the truth, you hit the nail on the head. The commanders had had their fill by this time. They clamored for order. This is what they demanded here, a general law and order, because the army could not with problems of this magnitude.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And, General, just to follow up on that in order to achieve these goals, in order to take these necessary measures, it was -- these were not things that the military side could do, at least not alone. These were measures that the government was going to have to undertake. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, all the authorities were supposed to take measures, all the organs, all the bodies, because a greater involvement and imposition of order is what is demanded here because the army could no longer do the tasks it was given. So there's no politics here. We're not defining political goals. It's just that the problems that existed in the rear outside of the army had to be dealt with more vigorously because the commanders faced this big problem. They had to hold the lines and, in effect, defend the territory, whatever you want to define that territory as.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And the President introduced this concept of putsch. It bears noting, General, that two days after this meeting occurred you were out as commander of the HVO Main Staff. Is your departure, at least in part, linked to the problems and the difficulties identified by your commanders that are contained in this document?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Partly, yes. At the meeting in Split I demanded changes, an overall change. Well, changing of me -- well, changes, and of Mate Boban. And again not trying to influence the politics because it had nothing to do with it, but the structure of the municipalities had to be improved and strengthened, and the conscription, controlling of smuggling, and so on. I don't want now to go into how -- to what extent it was really possible to do that, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, I want to look at the next two documents in tandem because they are related. They're both dated the following day, the 8th of November, 1993. The first is P06534, and this document is a Paket communication issued by General Petkovic. It's an order for offensive combat operations.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if you allow me regarding this document. I have a note for the record. This document is really a document that was sent via Paket radio. We do not see Mr. Petkovic's signature here, but let me draw your attention to the fact that General Praljak has just told us that on that day, the 8th of November, General Petkovic was in Split visiting his family. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, now, this is the 8th of November. This is before you've departed for Zagreb. Were you aware of this order being issued by General Petkovic on the 8th of November?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Your Honours. This is not a document issued by Mr. Petkovic, and I explained the reasons for that a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is true that on the 8th of November Mr. Petkovic was not in the Main Staff because he happened to be in Split, and I know that for certain. Whether he had left the day before, on the 7th -- before I went to Tomislavgrad we agreed that he should go there -- And in response of your question, I didn't know about this order, regardless of who compiled it, because on the 8th of November, after the meeting in Tomislavgrad, I stayed on and waited for General Roso and was with him until late at night until I went to Citluk where I spent the night.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: On this date, the 8th of November, you were at the Main Staff headquarters of the HVO; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, I wasn't there, but had I been given this kind of order -- or if I had to sign it, then I would certainly have done so, have signed it. So attack, link up those units, because their offensive was moving on, continuing.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, General -- so are you saying you never saw this at the time?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And you were not aware of it at the time?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right. Item number 3 says that the Mostar military district is to carry out offensive operations with smaller formations in the areas of Salakovac, Bijelo Polje, the town of Mostar, Blagaj. Shell the town of Mostar selectively at various intervals." General, were you aware of whether Mostar was shelled on the 8th of November pursuant to this order?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Stringer, well, one should see when this order was sent out. If it was sent out on the 8th it might have been sent out at noon, and I see it says 0300 hours or whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right. Well, maybe the next document will shed a little bit of light on this. The next one is P06524. And now this is a document, again a Paket communication, bearing the stamp of the HVO, and this is Brigadier Lasic, and he's making a reference to order number 02-2/1-01-3365, which, General, does match the document number or the order number for the previous document, the Paket communication over General Petkovic's name. So let me ask you this: Were you aware of this order of General Lasic forwarding the previous order down the chain of command?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, I wasn't aware of that. I see that it arrived at 12.00 noon on the 8th of November, as it says here, or it was sent out at 12.00 noon. Well, that's more probable. Well, I don't really know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: We see in item number 1, again the order is to "all units must plan to launch offensive operations without delay." Then item number 2 orders them to: "Plan offensive operations with small units in the following areas Salakovac, Bijelo Polje, Mostar, and Blagaj." And then again it says: "Shell the city of Mostar selectively at different time intervals." And the next one it says: "Sector commanders shall organise meetings with units up to the level of battalions and other independent units in brigades and issue tasks proceeding from this order in the order of the HVO Main Staff commander issued at the meeting in Tomislavgrad on 7 November 1993." Now, General, just starting with that last point, we'll work backwards, you were the HVO Main Staff commander. You were present at the meeting in Tomislavgrad on 7 November 1993. What's the order that you issued at the Tomislavgrad meeting on 7 November 1993?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't issue any -- any order, and quite obviously there's a mistake here, because it's a communication, communique, and it was probably written as being an order, but it wasn't, in fact, an order.
